summary: Paris-based startup Amo, co-founded by Zenly co-founder Antoine Martin and nine other former Zenly people, is launching ID, an iOS social app built around customizable, spatial profile canvases that friends can add to. Amo raised $20 million in 2023 without a product or revenue, and aims to counter passive, algorithmic social feeds and loneliness. The app deliberately limits time spent by closing itself after you view the last notification card.
one_line: Zenly founder Antoine Martin's startup Amo, backed by $20 million, launches ID, an iOS social app of creative, editable friend profile canvases.
key_facts: Amo is a small Paris-based team that spent most of 2023 building a new iOS social app called ID, launching on the day of the article.
Amo was co-founded by Antoine Martin, who co-founded Zenly with Alexis Bonillo; Martin is Amo's CEO.

Amo has 10 co-founders, all former Zenly people, including Corentin Kerisit, Michael Goldenstein, Claire Pluvinage, Charly Delaroche, Julien Martin, Quentin Perez, Nicolas Fallourd, Alexis Druon and Jean-Baptiste Dalido.
Snap spent more than $200 million to acquire Zenly; at its peak 18 million different users opened the app every day, before Snap shut it down as part of cost-cutting.
Amo closed a $20 million (€18 million) round in February or March at a valuation around €100 million, led by New Wave with Coatue and DST Global Partners, plus 80 angel investors.
The round was unusual because it happened during a 2023 VC funding downturn, for a mobile consumer startup with no revenue and no product out yet.
ID gives each user an empty whiteboard profile that can be filled with stickers, photos from the photo library, text or drawings; photos are automatically cut out using PhotoRoom's technology.
Friends can see each other's profiles and add things to them; users can also copy content from other profiles into their own sticker library, and you can see who originally created a sticker.
Every object on an ID profile can be moved, resized and rotated, making the profile a spatial canvas that can be zoomed.
When you reach the last notification card, ID shows a message saying "get some fresh air" and then the app closes itself.
Martin says Amo is prioritizing scale and now believes an indestructible company needs 100 million daily active users, not 18 million.
Martin cites the World Health Organization's "loneliness epidemic" as motivation, arguing existing social apps are passive and don't have users' best interests in mind.
Amo shipped ID eight or nine months after the company's launch, aiming to learn by building in public.
